items.title: bug: desktop auto-update kills its own backend via _kill_stale_dashboard_processes

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

items.body:
## Bug Description

When launching `hermes desktop`, the in-app auto-update mechanism (`applyUpdatesPosixInApp`) runs `hermes update`, which calls `_kill_stale_dashboard_processes()`. That function scans the process table for anything matching `hermes dashboard` and sends SIGTERM — **including the `hermes dashboard` process that the Electron app itself spawned as its backend**.

This creates a boot→kill→reboot→crash loop where the desktop can never stay connected.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Be 1+ commits behind origin/main
2. Run `hermes desktop`
3. Desktop spawns `hermes dashboard --no-open --tui --host 127.0.0.1 --port <random>` as its backend
4. Backend becomes ready, desktop connects successfully
5. Desktop renderer detects pending updates and triggers `hermes:updates:apply`
6. `applyUpdatesPosixInApp` runs `hermes update --yes`
7. `hermes update` calls `_kill_stale_dashboard_processes()` which SIGTERMs the desktop's own backend
8. Desktop detects backend died, restarts it
9. Update rebuilds the desktop app, triggering another restart
10. Final backend starts but then crashes: `⚡ Interrupted during API call`
11. All subsequent `hermes:api` IPC calls timeout: `Error: Timed out connecting to Hermes backend after 15000ms`

## Root Cause

`_find_stale_dashboard_pids()` in `hermes_cli/main.py` (line ~7131) only exempts its own PID:

```python
if any(p in command for p in patterns) and pid != self_pid:
    dashboard_pids.append(pid)
```

It does not account for the case where `hermes update` was invoked by the Electron desktop app, whose child `hermes dashboard` process should NOT be killed.

## Desktop Log Evidence

```
[hermes] [boot] Hermes backend is ready. Finalizing desktop startup
[hermes] [updates] update: Updating Hermes (git + dependencies)…
... (update runs) ...
[hermes] Hermes backend exited (SIGTERM)
[hermes] Hermes backend exited (SIGTERM)
[hermes] [updates] update: ⟲ Stopping 2 dashboard process(es) (the running backend no longer matches the updated frontend)
[hermes] [updates] update: ✓ stopped PID 717447
[hermes] [updates] update: ✓ stopped PID 717805
... (rebuild happens, desktop reboots) ...
[hermes] [boot] Hermes backend is ready. Finalizing desktop startup
[hermes] ⚡ Interrupted during API call.
```

After this, every IPC call from the renderer fails with:

```
Error occurred in handler for 'hermes:api': Error: Timed out connecting to Hermes backend after 15000ms
```

## Suggested Fix

Any of:

1. **Exclusion PID list**: `_find_stale_dashboard_pids()` accepts an optional `exclude_pids` parameter. The desktop passes its backend child PID.
2. **Env var marker**: The desktop sets `HERMES_DESKTOP_MANAGED=1` on its spawned backend process. `_find_stale_dashboard_pids()` skips processes with that env var.
3. **Desktop handles post-update restart**: Instead of having `hermes update` kill dashboards, the desktop kills its own backend after the update completes and restarts it cleanly.

## Environment

- Hermes v0.15.1
- Linux 7.0.10-201.fc44.x86_64 (Aurora/Fedora immutable)
- Electron 40.9.3
- Python 3.11.14

## Workaround

Run `hermes update` separately before launching the desktop, so the auto-update has nothing to trigger on:

```bash
hermes update --yes
hermes desktop
```

items.title: [Bug]: `hermes desktop` build fails on Linux with `ENOENT: rename 'electron' -> 'Hermes'` when the cached Electron download is corrupt

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

items.body:
### Bug Description

Launching the native desktop app with `hermes desktop` on Ubuntu 24.04 fails
during the electron-builder packaging step. The renderer build (Vite/tsc)
completes fine, but `electron-builder --dir` aborts with an `ENOENT` while
renaming the unpacked `electron` binary to the product name `Hermes`:

```
⨯ ENOENT: no such file or directory, rename
  '.../apps/desktop/release/linux-unpacked/electron' ->
  '.../apps/desktop/release/linux-unpacked/Hermes'
✗ Desktop GUI build failed
  Run manually:  cd apps/desktop && npm run pack
```

The error message points at a rename inside `release/linux-unpacked/`, which
makes it look like a stale-output-directory or permissions problem. It is
neither. The underlying cause is a **corrupt cached Electron distribution zip**
in the per-user Electron download cache. Because `hermes desktop` re-runs the
same broken extraction on every invocation, the desktop app is **permanently
unlaunchable** until the user manually deletes a cache file they have no way of
knowing about.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Be on Linux (reproduced on Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.17, Node 24.12, npm 11.6,
   Electron 40.9.3, electron-builder 26.8.1).
2. Have a corrupt/truncated Electron zip in the per-user cache. This happens
   naturally when a prior download is interrupted (network drop, Ctrl-C, full
   disk) and leaves a partial or duplicated file at:
   ```
   ~/.cache/electron/electron-v40.9.3-linux-x64.zip
   ```
3. Run the documented entry point:
   ```bash
   hermes desktop
   ```
4. Observe the renderer build succeed, then the packaging step fail with the
   `ENOENT … rename 'electron' -> 'Hermes'` error above.
5. Confirm the cache zip is corrupt:
   ```bash
   unzip -t ~/.cache/electron/electron-v40.9.3-linux-x64.zip
   # warning: NNNNNNNN extra bytes at beginning or within zipfile
   # -> integrity test exits non-zero (CORRUPT)
   ```
6. Re-running `hermes desktop` repeats the identical failure — it never
   self-recovers.

### Expected Behavior

`hermes desktop` should produce a launchable desktop app, or recover
automatically when its own build cache is the problem. A corrupt entry in the
Electron download cache should not permanently wedge every future run. At
minimum, the failure should be self-healing: detect the bad cache entry, purge
it, and let electron-builder re-download a clean distribution.

### Actual Behavior

The packaged build fails on the final rename and exits non-zero:

```
• packaging       platform=linux arch=x64 electron=40.9.3 appOutDir=release/linux-unpacked
• detected workspace root for project using lock file
⨯ ENOENT: no such file or directory, rename
  '.../release/linux-unpacked/electron' -> '.../release/linux-unpacked/Hermes'
```

The half-written `release/linux-unpacked/` directory is left in a
plausible-looking partial state — it contains `LICENSE.electron.txt`,
`chrome-sandbox`, the `*.pak` files, and a few `.so` libraries — but the 193 MB
`electron` binary that should be renamed to `Hermes` is **missing entirely**.
Casual inspection suggests "the build mostly worked," which masks the real
cause. Every subsequent `hermes desktop` re-runs the same broken extraction
from the same corrupt cache, so the app never launches.

### Affected Component

Setup / Installation

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

N/A (CLI only)

### Debug Report

```shell
Report       https://paste.rs/lhIJC
agent.log    https://paste.rs/JboKu
gateway.log  https://paste.rs/NuWcN
```

### Operating System

Ubuntu 24.04

### Python Version

3.12.3

### Hermes Version

0.15.1

### Additional Logs / Traceback (optional)


electron-builder does **not** package the Electron binary from
`node_modules/electron/dist`. It runs `app-builder unpack-electron`, which
extracts the Electron distribution **from a zip stored in the per-user download
cache** (`~/.cache/electron/electron-v<ver>-<os>-<arch>.zip`).

download. Verified directly:

(`LICENSE`, `*.pak`, `chrome-sandbox`, a handful of `.so` files) but the large
`electron` binary never lands. electron-builder then tries to rename the
now-missing `electron` to `Hermes` and dies with `ENOENT`.

The stale-`linux-unpacked/`-directory hypothesis was tested and **disproven**:
cleaning the output directory and re-running still failed because
`unpack-electron` re-extracted the same corrupt zip. The load-bearing fix is to
**validate and purge the corrupt cache entry, then retry** — at which point
electron-builder re-downloads a clean copy and the build produces a launchable
193 MB `Hermes` binary (confirmed end-to-end).

Contributing factor: a previously interrupted pack can also leave a partial
`release/linux-unpacked/` that poisons the next run's rename, so making the pack
step idempotent (wiping the unpacked dir before staging) is a useful complement.

items.title: Desktop: onboarding overlay re-appears on every app restart
items.body:
## Description

After completing initial setup (bootstrap + onboarding provider config), closing and re-opening the Hermes Desktop app shows the onboarding/install prompt again, as if the user never completed configuration.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Install Hermes Desktop and complete first-launch bootstrap (`install.sh`) + onboarding (provider/model setup)
2. Confirm the main chat UI loads correctly
3. Close the app (Cmd+Q or window close)
4. Re-open Hermes Desktop
5. **Actual:** The onboarding overlay ("Add a provider credential before sending your first message") or install overlay reappears instead of the main chat UI
6. Closing and re-opening again repeats the cycle indefinitely

## Expected Behavior

After successful first-time setup, subsequent launches should go straight to the main chat UI without re-prompting for provider/install configuration.

## Root Cause (traced)

There are **two** overlays that gate the main UI, and both have persistence issues:

### 1. `DesktopOnboardingOverlay` (primary issue)

The overlay uses `localStorage['hermes-desktop-onboarded-v1']` as an initial optimistic cache, but **re-evaluates every time the gateway opens** via `evaluateRuntimeReadiness()`, which calls:

- `setup.status` — returns `provider_configured: boolean`
- `setup.runtime_check` — returns `ok: boolean`

When the backend reports `provider_configured: false` (or the runtime check fails), the store resets `configured → false` and shows the overlay again, **overwriting the localStorage cache**.

So even though `localStorage` reads `'1'`, the store re-evaluates and flips it to `false` on every boot.

**Relevant code paths:**

- `src/store/onboarding.ts` → `refreshOnboarding()` line 385-407: calls `checkRuntime()`, and if `!runtime.ready`, sets `configured: false` + `writeCachedConfigured(false)`
- `src/components/desktop-onboarding-overlay.tsx` line 153: `if (onboarding.configured === true && !onboarding.manual) return null` — so returning users get the overlay
- `src/lib/runtime-readiness.ts` line 82-138: `interpretRuntimeReadiness()` — determines readiness from gateway responses

### 2. `DesktopInstallOverlay` (edge case)

The bootstrap-complete marker (`~/.hermes/hermes-agent/.hermes-bootstrap-complete`) is checked correctly in `main.cjs` via `isBootstrapComplete()` and should suppress re-install. However, if the venv is missing, the marker alone won't suffice — the check also requires `fileExists(getVenvPython(VENV_ROOT))`.

## Environment

- macOS 26.5 (M1 Pro)
- Hermes Desktop v0.15.1
- Hermes Agent head (self-built from source)

## Additional Context

Full trace available at `electron/main.cjs` → `resolveHermesBackend()`, `isBootstrapComplete()`, and `src/store/onboarding.ts` → `refreshOnboarding()`.

The core issue is that `localStorage` is an unreliable persistence mechanism for onboarding state — any gateway response discrepancy resets it. A durable marker on disk (similar to the bootstrap-complete marker) or a dedicated `setup.onboarded` config flag would fix this.

items.title: [FEATURE] Multi-model deliberation planner — /council command with 3-stage pipeline

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

labels.name: sweeper:not-planned
labels.description: Sweeper: closed per standing maintainer policy (design direction)

items.body:
## Summary

Add a `/council` command that orchestrates multi-model deliberation for structured implementation planning. Three different frontier models independently propose plans, an anonymized critic evaluates them, and a chairman model synthesizes the best approach into a unified output with file manifest, execution steps, risk register, and vote matrix.

## Motivation

Hermes users currently type planning requests directly to a single model. The output quality depends entirely on that model's training and the user's prompt skill. A council deliberation addresses three problems:

1. **Single-model blind spots** — models have different strengths (GLM excels at SWE-Bench, Kimi at reasoning chains, MiniMax at sparse-attention recall). A council captures the best of each.
2. **No structured output** — a single model returns whatever format it chooses. The council produces a standardized plan with file manifest, risk register, and vote matrix.
3. **No peer review** — plans are never critiqued before execution, so gaps in edge cases, security, or error handling go unnoticed.

## Design

### Architecture

3-stage pipeline in `agent/council.py`:

**Stage 1 — Propose:** N proposer models (configurable, default 3) each generate an independent implementation plan. Two modes:
- **Flat mode** (fast, ~40s): each proposer is a single API call
- **Subagent mode** (thorough, ~2.5 min): each proposer runs as a Hermes `delegate_task` with `role=orchestrator`, can delegate subtasks to cheaper models

**Stage 2 — Critique:** An anonymized peer review evaluates all plans on correctness, completeness, and efficiency. Skips automatically when only one plan exists.

**Stage 3 — Chairman:** Synthesizes plans + critiques into a unified output with:
- Consensus score
- Selected approach with justification
- File manifest (file, action, rationale, proposed by)
- Execution steps (numbered)
- Risk register (risk, likelihood, mitigation, flagged by)
- Disagreements resolved
- Proposal breakdown table (per-proposer scores)

### Key design decisions

| Decision | Choice | Rationale |
|----------|--------|-----------|
| Proposer concurrency | Configurable, auto-derives from `delegation.max_concurrent_children` | Prevents overloading provider rate limits |
| Retry policy | Geometric backoff 5×attempt², max 3 attempts | Cloud providers have transient latency spikes |
| Content validation | Min 15 lines, 500 chars, structural markers required | Rejects "I analyzed the code" stubs |
| State persistence | Full pipeline state saved before chairman stage | Enables `/council resume` on failure |
| Single-plan skip | Single valid plan auto-skips critique | No peer comparison possible with 1 plan |
| Pipeline timeout | 2400s (40 min) guard on total execution | Prevents runaway pipelines |

### Resilience built-in

The same architecture includes production guardrails because cloud LLM calls fail:

- **Retry with geometric backoff** — TimeoutError and empty content are retried (5s, 15s, 30s delays). Cloud providers routinely drop the first call during peak load.
- **Content validation gate** — rejects output under 15 lines, 500 chars, or lacking structural markers (triple backtick code blocks, `## Plan` headings).
- **State persistence + `/council resume`** — full pipeline state saved before the chairman stage. If chairman crashes, `run_resume()` loads saved plans+critiques and re-runs only the chairman.
- **Pipeline timeout guard** — 2400s upper bound on total execution prevents runaway pipelines.
- **Dynamic timeouts** — each stage's timeout scales with input size. Floor values: proposer 120s, critique 120s, chairman 300s.

## Interface

### New commands

| Command | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `/council <task>` | Run full council deliberation (default mode) |
| `/council plan <task>` | Explicit plan subcommand |
| `/council status` | Show current council configuration |
| `/council resume [path]` | Resume failed council from saved state |

### Config (`config.yaml`)

```yaml
council:
  enabled: true
  default_mode: plan
  subagent_delegation: true
  max_concurrent_calls: 2
  pipeline_timeout_seconds: 2400
  proposers:
    - provider: ollama-cloud
      model: glm-5.1:cloud
    - provider: ollama-cloud
      model: kimi-k2.6:cloud
    - provider: ollama-cloud
      model: minimax-m2.5:cloud
  subagents:
    fast:
      provider: ollama-cloud
      model: deepseek-v4-flash:cloud
    lightweight:
      provider: ollama-cloud
      model: gemma4:31b:cloud
  critic:
    provider: ollama-cloud
    model: minimax-m3:cloud
  chairman:
    provider: ollama-cloud
    model: minimax-m3:cloud
  peer_review: true
  anonymize_reviews: true
  preflight:
    enabled: true
    timeout_seconds: 30
    min_proposers: 2
    check_interval_hours: 24
  min_plan_lines: 15
  min_plan_chars: 500
  max_retries: 2
```

## Files Changed

| File | Lines | What |
|------|-------|------|
| `agent/council.py` | +1,214 | `CouncilOrchestrator` — 3-stage pipeline, retry, validation, state, resume |
| `cli.py` | +182 | CLI handlers for `/council plan\|status\|resume` |
| `gateway/run.py` | +139 | Gateway dispatchers for `/council` via Discord/Telegram/etc |

items.body:
## Feature Description

Add optional `model` and `provider` parameters to the `delegate_task` tool so subagents can run under a different model than the parent conversation.

## Motivation

The parent agent might be on a text-only model (e.g., DeepSeek-v4-flash), but specific subtasks — especially vision reasoning — require a model with native vision support (Claude, GPT-4o, Gemini). Currently there is no way to give a subagent a different model, forcing users to either:

1. Accept degraded vision quality through a text-only vision pipeline (Gemma4 → text description → reasoning)
2. Swap their main model entirely (expensive per-turn cost)
3. Work around it with separate Hermes profiles or tmux spawning (high overhead)

The `cronjob` tool already supports per-job model overrides (`model: {provider: "...", model: "..."}`), proving the infrastructure is there — it just wasnt wired into `delegate_task`.

## Proposed Solution

Add a `model` parameter (same shape as the cronjob tool) to `delegate_task`:

```json
"model": {
  "type": "object",
  "description": "Optional per-subagent model override. If provider is omitted, the current provider is used.",
  "properties": {
    "provider": {"type": "string"},
    "model": {"type": "string"}
  }
}
```

When set, the subagent initializes with the specified model/provider instead of inheriting the parents. When omitted, current behavior is preserved.

## Alternatives Considered

- **Swap main model** — works but is heavy; every turn pays the vision-model token cost even when unnecessary.
- **Separate Hermes profile** — works but requires tmux spawning and manual context relay. No isolation benefits of `delegate_task`.
- **Vision pipeline** — functional for simple image checks, but the game-of-telephone effect (vision model → text description → parent reasoning) loses fidelity and cant do precise spatial reasoning or reading small text.

## Implementation Notes

The `delegation.*` config section already exists in `config.yaml`. The `cronjob` tool schema already demonstrates the pattern. The subagent creation path in `run_agent.py` / `agent/` already accepts model/provider overrides — this is wiring an existing capability through the tool schema and the `delegate_task` dispatcher.

## Bug Description
On Hermes Desktop for Windows, pasting a screenshot into the chat composer attaches the same image twice.

The duplicate attachments are saved as two separate files under:

`C:\Users\ianar\AppData\Roaming\Hermes\composer-images\`

Example from one paste:

- `composer_2026-06-02_18-33-43-065_224319.png`
- `composer_2026-06-02_18-33-43-065_9c6f14.png`

Both appear to be the same screenshot.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. On Windows 11, take/copy a screenshot to the clipboard.
2. Open Hermes Desktop.
3. Paste the screenshot into the chat composer.
4. Observe the image appears as two attachments.

## Expected Behavior
The pasted screenshot should attach once.

## Actual Behavior
The pasted screenshot attaches twice.

## Suspected Cause
The composer paste handler extracts image blobs from both `clipboard.items` and `clipboard.files`.

On Windows/Electron, the same clipboard image can appear through both paths. The current dedupe uses `Set<Blob>()`, which only dedupes the same object reference. Electron may provide two different Blob/File objects containing the same image, so both are saved.

Relevant code observed locally:

- `apps/desktop/src/app/chat/composer/index.tsx`
  - `handlePaste`
  - calls `extractClipboardImageBlobs(event.clipboardData)`

- `apps/desktop/src/app/chat/composer/text-utils.ts`
  - `extractClipboardImageBlobs`
  - checks both `clipboard.items` and `clipboard.files`
  - dedupes with `Set<Blob>()`

## Possible Fix
Either:

- Prefer `clipboard.items` and skip `clipboard.files` if image blobs were already found, or
- Dedupe by image metadata/content-like signature such as `type + size + name + lastModified`, rather than Blob object identity.

- App: Hermes Desktop
- Repo: NousResearch/hermes-agent

items.title: Desktop Skills & Tools toggle silently fails for platform-restricted toolsets (false-success PUT)

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

items.body:
**Summary:** In the desktop app, toggling a platform-restricted toolset (e.g. `discord_admin`) shows it enabled but it reverts on navigation and never persists. The PUT returns success even though the write is silently discarded.

**Repro**
1. Desktop app → Skills & Tools.
2. Toggle "Discord Server Admin" (`discord_admin`) on.
3. Navigate to another page and back.

**Expected:** stays enabled, or the toggle is unavailable with a reason.
**Actual:** reverts to off; no error; the PUT returned `{ok:true, enabled:true}`.

**Root cause** (read-only trace; line numbers verified against `upstream/main`)
- The desktop toggle PUTs `/api/tools/toolsets/{name}` with no platform arg (`apps/desktop/src/hermes.ts:337-346`); the backend hardcodes the `cli` platform (`hermes_cli/web_server.py:5877,5883`).
- `discord_admin` is platform-restricted to `{"discord"}` (`hermes_cli/tools_config.py:136`), so `_save_platform_tools` filters it out of the `cli` set before writing (`tools_config.py:1440-1443`) — the enable is silently dropped.
- The endpoint still returns `{ok:true, enabled:true}` (`web_server.py:5884`) → false success; the optimistic UI shows on.
- Read-back reads `platform_toolsets.cli` (`web_server.py:5831-5835`), where it was never written → the row reverts on nav.
- The row is offered as toggleable because `_get_effective_configurable_toolsets` doesn't filter by platform restriction (`tools_config.py:149-172`).

**Three distinct defects**
1. False-positive success: a write filtered out by platform restriction still returns `{ok:true, enabled:true}`. (Core bug.)
2. Mismatched display: platform-restricted toolsets appear as toggleable rows in a GUI whose only write scope (`cli`) can never hold them.
3. No platform targeting: the desktop endpoint can't write `platform_toolsets.<non-cli>`.

**Suggested fix (minimal):** return the *effective* persisted state after save so the UI can't show a false success, and either hide/disable toggles for toolsets not allowed on the GUI's platform or label them "managed via CLI." A platform param is the fuller fix.

**Workaround:** enable via CLI — `hermes tools enable discord_admin --platform discord` — which writes `platform_toolsets.discord` and persists across restarts.

items.title: Per-model compression threshold overrides

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

items.body:
## Problem

`compression.threshold` is global, but different models have different context windows. A single ratio forces compromise — 0.5 is reasonable for 200K models (triggers at 100K) but absurd for 1M models (500K).

Current workaround: users override `model.context_length` to an artificially low value to control when compaction fires. This is fragile and breaks if you switch models.

## Proposal

Allow optional `compression` overrides in the `model` config section:

```yaml
model:
  default: deepseek-v4-pro
  provider: deepseek
  context_length: 1000000
  compression:
    threshold: 0.15   # triggers at 150K tokens
    target_ratio: 0.2
```

Falls back to global `compression.threshold` when per-model override is absent. Fully backward-compatible.

## Use case

Price-conscious users on large-context models want compaction to fire proportionally to what they actually need, not to the model's maximum. A personal agent on DeepSeek doesn't need 500K tokens of live context — but switching the global threshold down would make Claude/OpenAI models compact too aggressively.

## Affected config sections

- `model` — add optional `compression` sub-key
- `compression` — unchanged, remains the global default

items.title: httpx/OpenAI SDK hangs on IPv6 when connecting to provider endpoints (e.g. opencode.ai) — suggest happy-eyeballs fix

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

items.body:
## Problem

When Hermes connects to an OpenAI-compatible provider endpoint (e.g. `opencode.ai/zen/go/v1`), the OpenAI Python SDK / httpx can **hang indefinitely** during `client.chat.completions.create(...)` because it tries **IPv6 first** and the IPv6 connection stalls.

The DNS for many provider endpoints (Cloudflare-backed) resolves to both IPv6 and IPv4 addresses. On systems where IPv6 connectivity is broken or slow (common on macOS, certain Docker setups, or networks without proper IPv6 routing), httpx attempts IPv6 → hangs → takes a very long time to fall back to IPv4.

### Evidence

```
# curl (happy-eyeballs: tries both, IPv4 wins immediately)
curl → IPv4: 1.49s  ✅   |   IPv6: TIMEOUT (>15s) ❌

# OpenAI Python SDK (httpx): tries IPv6 first → hangs
client.chat.completions.create(...) → SIGALRM killed at 10s

# After forcing IPv4 via monkey-patch socket.getaddrinfo:
client.chat.completions.create(...) → 2-3s ✅
```

### Impact

- **"Initializing agent..."** message hangs during `AIAgent.__init__()` → `_create_openai_client()`
- `hermes -z` one-shot mode hangs
- TUI interactive mode hangs on first turn
- Error logs show nothing — it is a silent hang, not a crash
- User-visible: agent appears frozen

### Root Cause

The `httpx.Client` used by the OpenAI SDK does not seem to implement proper **happy-eyeballs** (RFC 8305 / RFC 6555) fallback. Curl does this correctly (1.5s total), but the Python httpx/OpenAI stack gets stuck on the first IPv6 connection attempt.

### Workaround

Setting `network.force_ipv4: true` in `~/.hermes/config.yaml` works around the issue:

```yaml
network:
  force_ipv4: true
```

### Suggested Fix

- Add happy-eyeballs / connection-level timeout to httpx transport in `_build_keepalive_http_client()` (`run_agent.py:2953`)
- Or properly implement `network.force_ipv4` flag across ALL connection paths (not just OpenAI client but also auxiliary client connections)
- Or add socket-level connection timeout to prevent indefinite hangs

### Environment

- Hermes v0.15.1
- macOS 14.7.8 (ARM64)
- Provider: opencode-go / deepseek-v4-flash
- Python 3.11.14
- OpenAI SDK 2.24.0

items.title: Desktop long prompts can visually cover assistant output because sticky user messages are unbounded

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

items.body:
## Summary

Desktop user messages are rendered as sticky, high-z-index elements at the top of the thread. For long prompts, the read-only user bubble has no max-height or internal scroll boundary, so the prompt can occupy the visible thread and cover the assistant/tool output below it. The response can exist in the session/DOM, but the user sees what looks like a missing or blank assistant response.

This was validated against a clean upstream worktree, not a branded/local fork.

## Upstream validation

Source checked against `origin/main` at commit `c47b9d126f2f` in a detached worktree.

Pure source facts from `apps/desktop/src/components/assistant-ui/thread.tsx`:

- `StickyHumanMessageContainer` uses:
  - `sticky top-0 z-40`
  - `overflow-visible`
- The read-only user bubble path does not include a max-height or `overflow-y-auto` guard.
- The clean upstream component contained no local branding changes.

I added only a regression test to the clean upstream worktree, without applying the fix. The test failed on upstream as expected:

```text
> hermes@0.15.1 test:ui
> vitest run --environment jsdom src/components/assistant-ui/streaming.test.tsx

src/components/assistant-ui/streaming.test.tsx (10 tests | 1 failed)
× caps long sticky user prompts so they do not cover the assistant turn

AssertionError: expected 'composer-human-message standalone-gla…' to contain 'max-h-[min(22rem,45vh)]'

Expected: "max-h-[min(22rem,45vh)]"
Received: "composer-human-message standalone-glass relative flex w-full min-w-0 max-w-full flex-col gap-1.5 overflow-hidden rounded-xl border bg-(--dt-user-bubble) px-3 py-2 text-left shadow-composer border-(--ui-stroke-tertiary) pr-9 text-[length:var(--conversation-text-font-size)] leading-(--dt-line-height) text-foreground/95 transition-colors cursor-pointer hover:border-(--ui-stroke-secondary)"
```

The same test passes after adding the height/overflow guard to the read-only user bubble:

```text
> vitest run --environment jsdom src/components/assistant-ui/streaming.test.tsx
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  10 passed (10)
```

## Reproduction

1. Open Hermes Desktop.
2. Submit or load a session with a very long user prompt followed by assistant/tool output.
3. Scroll the thread near the response.
4. The sticky user message remains pinned at the top and can visually cover the assistant turn, making it appear as if the assistant response did not render.

## Expected behavior

Long sticky prompts should remain readable/editable, but they should not be able to consume the visible thread or cover subsequent assistant/tool output.

## Actual behavior

A long sticky user prompt can occupy the thread viewport and obscure assistant output below it.

## Root cause

The sticky user message container is intentionally pinned with `sticky top-0 z-40`, but the read-only prompt bubble is unbounded. The edit composer path has its own max-height, but the displayed user message path does not.

## Suggested fix

Add a bounded scroll region to the read-only user bubble. The minimal fix that passed the regression locally was:

```tsx
const bubbleClassName = cn(
  USER_BUBBLE_BASE_CLASS,
  'max-h-[min(22rem,45vh)] overscroll-contain overflow-y-auto border-(--ui-stroke-tertiary) pr-9 text-[length:var(--conversation-text-font-size)] leading-(--dt-line-height) text-foreground/95 transition-colors',
  !threadRunning && 'cursor-pointer hover:border-(--ui-stroke-secondary)'
)
```

Suggested regression test shape:

```tsx
function longUserMessage(): ThreadMessage {
  return {
    ...userMessage(),
    content: [
      {
        type: 'text',
        text: Array.from({ length: 80 }, (_, index) => `Long prompt line ${index + 1}`).join('\n')
      }
    ]
  } as ThreadMessage
}

function LongPromptHarness() {
  const runtime = useExternalStoreRuntime<ThreadMessage>({
    messages: [longUserMessage(), assistantMessage('Assistant answer remains visible', false)],
    isRunning: false,
    onNew: async () => {}
  })

  return (
    <AssistantRuntimeProvider runtime={runtime}>
      <Thread />
    </AssistantRuntimeProvider>
  )
}

it('caps long sticky user prompts so they do not cover the assistant turn', () => {
  const { container } = render(<LongPromptHarness />)

  const userBubble = within(container).getByRole('button', { name: 'Edit message' })
  expect(userBubble.className).toContain('max-h-[min(22rem,45vh)]')
  expect(userBubble.className).toContain('overflow-y-auto')
  expect(within(container).getByText('Assistant answer remains visible')).toBeTruthy()
})
```

## Notes

This is not an assistant/backend failure. The output can be present, but the UI makes it look absent because the sticky prompt is visually dominating the thread.

items.title: Oversized image (>8000px) permanently bricks a conversation thread — image guards check bytes, never pixel dimensions

labels.name: duplicate
labels.description: This issue or pull request already exists

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

items.body:
## Summary

A single oversized image (specifically one exceeding Anthropic's **8000px per-side dimension cap**) can permanently brick a conversation thread. Once such an image is baked into history (e.g. a `browser_vision` / `vision_analyze` tool-result), every subsequent turn replays it, Anthropic returns a **non-retryable HTTP 400**, and the session is wedged forever — the user sees `⚠️ The model provider failed after retries` on every message and the only recovery is manually un-pinning the session on disk.

This bit a live multi-agent deployment: one full-page dashboard screenshot (591×1280 *on disk*, but the inline vision tool-result was a tall full-page capture >8000px) bricked an agent's DM thread until the session was surgically un-pinned in `sessions.json`.

## Root cause: every image guard reasons about BYTES, never PIXELS

Anthropic enforces **two independent ceilings** per image:
1. **5 MB** encoded byte size → `"image exceeds 5 MB maximum"`
2. **8000px** longest side → `"image dimensions exceed max allowed size: 8000 pixels"`

Hermes only ever guards #1. A tall full-page screenshot can be **well under 5 MB yet far over 8000px** — e.g. 1200×12000 at 0.06 MB — so it slips through every guard:

- **`error_classifier._IMAGE_TOO_LARGE_PATTERNS`** matches `"image exceeds"` but NOT the dimension message → the 400 is never classified `image_too_large` → the shrink/retry path never fires → falls through to a generic non-retryable error → brick.
- **`conversation_compression.try_shrink_image_parts_in_messages`** (the reactive recovery) early-returns when `len(url) <= target_bytes` (4 MB). A tall <4 MB image is judged "not the oversized one", shrink returns `False`, and the retry re-sends the identical payload → still 400 → brick.
- **`vision_tools._resize_image_for_vision`** resizes purely by byte budget; it never inspects pixel dimensions, so even when invoked it wouldn't fix a dimension violation.
- **The embed-time proactive cap** in `vision_tools` only triggers on `len(data_url) > _EMBED_TARGET_BYTES` — a byte test — so a tall small-byte image is baked into immutable history un-resized.

Secondary finding: **Pillow was not installed in the gateway venv** and is an undeclared soft dependency. Without it, *all* image-resize recovery (old byte path included) silently no-ops.

## Reproduction

1. Capture/attach an image taller than 8000px but under 5 MB (any full-page screenshot of a long page).
2. It embeds into history un-resized.
3. Next message → Anthropic 400 `image dimensions exceed max allowed size: 8000 pixels`.
4. Classifier doesn't recognize it → non-retryable → thread bricked on every subsequent message.

## Fix (4 coordinated patches)

1. **`error_classifier.py`** — add dimension-cap patterns (`"dimensions exceed max allowed size"`, `"image dimensions exceed"`, `"max allowed size: 8000"`) to `_IMAGE_TOO_LARGE_PATTERNS` so the 400 is classified `image_too_large` and routed into the existing shrink/retry recovery.
2. **`vision_tools.py`** — add `_MAX_IMAGE_DIMENSION = 7900` + `_image_exceeds_dimension()` helper; make `_resize_image_for_vision` enforce a **pixel** ceiling (pre-cap longest side before the byte loop, preserving aspect ratio) in addition to the byte ceiling.
3. **`vision_tools.py`** (embed site) — trigger the proactive resize when the image exceeds the byte budget **OR** the pixel cap, so tall small-byte screenshots are shrunk before being baked into immutable history.
4. **`conversation_compression.py`** — make the reactive shrinker decode the image and shrink when **either** ceiling is exceeded, instead of gating purely on `len(url) > 4 MB`.

Plus: install Pillow into the gateway venv (and it should be a declared dependency, since without it none of this recovery functions).

## Verification

- 1200×12000 @ 0.06 MB → resized to **790×7900** (under cap). ✅
- 800×600 small image → untouched. ✅
- Reactive shrinker on a 0.07 MB / 1000×11000 tool-result (old gate would skip) → shrinks to **718×7900**, retry succeeds. ✅
- Classifier matches both the 8000px message and the legacy 5 MB byte message. ✅
- All three modules `py_compile` clean.

Impact: prevents one oversized image from bricking a thread for any agent on Anthropic models (the 8000px cap is non-retryable and immutable once in history).

items.title: [Bug]: TUI drops shift+letter capitalization
items.body:
In `hermes --tui` on Ghostty, hold Shift+A → you get `a`, not `A`. Shift+Enter for newlines still works, so the shift flag is being received — just not applied to printable characters.

**Why:** `ui-tui/packages/hermes-ink/src/ink/ink.tsx:1348` enables the kitty keyboard protocol, so Ghostty sends `\x1b[97;2u` for Shift+A. hermes-ink reduces that to `input='a'` + `key.shift=true`, but the composer's `useInput` handler in `ui-tui/src/components/textInput.tsx:1111` inserts `inp` without uppercasing on `k.shift`. You get the keycode, not the character.

**Fix (2 lines, `textInput.tsx` before `applyPrintableInsert`):**

```ts
if (k.shift && text.length === 1 && text >= 'a' && text <= 'z') {
  text = text.toUpperCase()
}
```

**Workaround:** classic `hermes` REPL doesn't have this issue — same backend, same session.

items.title: Circuit-breaker (gave_up) blocks are auto-resurrected by recompute_ready → deterministic-failure tasks loop forever

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

items.body:
## Summary

A kanban task that fails **deterministically** (e.g. assigned to a profile whose model can never satisfy the tool-use protocol) loops indefinitely despite `kanban.failure_limit`. In production we saw one batch of 10 cards accumulate **>5,400 `protocol_violation` runs in ~11 h**, hammering a local inference backend the whole time.

## Reproduction (what we hit)

1. A task was assigned to a profile whose model is served with a small context window (a local NPU/Ollama backend capped at 4096 tokens). Hermes reports `minimum_context=64000` for its tool-use agent loop:
   ```
   Ollama runtime context too small for Hermes tool use:
   runtime_context=4096  minimum_context=64000  estimated_request_tokens=25639  tool_count=39
   ```
2. The worker can't run the loop, exits `rc=0` **without** calling `kanban_complete`/`kanban_block`.
3. The dispatcher correctly classifies this as a `protocol_violation` and force-trips the breaker at `effective_limit:1`:
   ```json
   {"failures": 1, "effective_limit": 1, "limit_source": "dispatcher",
    "error": "worker exited cleanly (rc=0) without calling kanban_complete or kanban_block — protocol violation",
    "trigger_outcome": "crashed"}
   ```
   → emits `gave_up`, task → `blocked`.
4. **`recompute_ready()` immediately promotes the blocked card back to `ready`, resetting `consecutive_failures=0`.** The sticky-block guard (`_has_sticky_block`, added in #28712) only protects *worker-initiated* `kanban_block`, not dispatcher `gave_up` blocks.
5. Card is re-dispatched → identical crash → loop. `consecutive_failures` is reset every cycle, so no limit ever sticks. We observed equal counts of `gave_up` and `promoted` events (100/100 over ~12 min) confirming the oscillation.

Net effect: neither `failure_limit` nor a container restart stops the loop. The only ways out we found were reassigning the task to a capable profile (`hermes kanban reassign … --reclaim`) or archiving it.

## Expected

A circuit-breaker `gave_up` block should be **sticky** (surface to a human), or there should be a lifetime-attempt cap independent of the resettable `consecutive_failures`. A deterministically-failing task must not re-spawn forever.

## Suggested fix

In `hermes_cli/kanban_db.py::recompute_ready` (~L2450-2504): only auto-promote blocks whose cause is a **parent dependency** completing. Treat a `gave_up`-originated block the same as a worker-initiated `kanban_block` (skip auto-promotion until an explicit `unblock`). Alternatively, track a non-resettable lifetime attempt counter and stop dispatching past a ceiling.

Relevant code:
- `recompute_ready` auto-promotion of `blocked` + `consecutive_failures=0` reset — `hermes_cli/kanban_db.py` (~L2450-2504)
- `gave_up` / protocol-violation classification in the stale-reclaim dispatcher pass — `hermes_cli/kanban_db.py` (~L4860-4960)
- sticky-block guard that currently excludes circuit-breaker blocks — `_has_sticky_block` (#28712)

items.title: [Bug]: Nix build broken — `hermes-desktop-renderer` npmDepsHash is out of date

items.body:
## Bug Description

The `hermes-desktop-renderer` derivation (in `nix/desktop.nix`) has a stale `npmDepsHash`. Building the Nix flake fails with:

```
error: hash mismatch in fixed-output derivation '/nix/store/...-npm-deps.drv':
         specified: sha256-7W9ObYz08yDMtybY8+RkUXkKVsJXINLl0qBUB91hpao=
            got:    sha256-hLmt1p1QPkC2jJKeZ6DGfwkPZSanMwV/scnTZ42ddk8=
error: Cannot build '/nix/store/...-hermes-desktop-renderer-0.15.1.drv'.
error: Cannot build '/nix/store/...-hermes-desktop-0.15.1.drv'.
```

This is the same class of bug as the resolved #12965, #15244, #15272 (`hermes-web`) and #15314, #19760 (`hermes-tui`), now recurring on `hermes-desktop-renderer`.

## Root Cause

`apps/desktop/package-lock.json` was committed in `51c68d4ab1a9` ("Add Hermes desktop app", #20059) but the `npmDepsHash` pinned in `nix/desktop.nix:18` does not match the lockfile content. The hash has been wrong since the desktop app was introduced; nothing on `main` has built it cleanly on a fresh store.

Stale hash at [`nix/desktop.nix:18`](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/main/nix/desktop.nix#L18):
```nix
hash = "sha256-7W9ObYz08yDMtybY8+RkUXkKVsJXINLl0qBUB91hpao=";
```

Actual hash for the committed `apps/desktop/package-lock.json` (fetcherVersion = 2):
```
sha256-hLmt1p1QPkC2jJKeZ6DGfwkPZSanMwV/scnTZ42ddk8=
```

## Steps to Reproduce

On a clean Nix store:

```bash
nix build github:NousResearch/hermes-agent#hermes-desktop
# or any flake build that pulls in hermesDesktop, e.g.
nix flake check
```

Both fail with the hash mismatch above.

## Expected Behavior

`hermes-desktop` (and `hermes-desktop-renderer`) build successfully on `main`.

## Actual Behavior

Build fails during `npmConfigHook` consistency check between `apps/desktop/package-lock.json` and the prefetched npm deps cache.

## Affected Component

- Setup / Installation (Nix flake build)

## Operating System

NixOS (any) — affects all platforms; the failure is in the fixed-output derivation, not platform-dependent.

## Proposed Fix

Update `nix/desktop.nix:18` from:

```nix
hash = "sha256-7W9ObYz08yDMtybY8+RkUXkKVsJXINLl0qBUB91hpao=";
```

to:

```nix
hash = "sha256-hLmt1p1QPkC2jJKeZ6DGfwkPZSanMwV/scnTZ42ddk8=";
```

Same remediation as previous occurrences (e.g. #15314). Longer term: the existing `nix/scripts/update-nix-hashes.ts` (or equivalent) could be extended to cover `apps/desktop/package-lock.json`, and a CI guard added to flag drift between any tracked `package-lock.json` and its corresponding `npmDepsHash`.

## Related Issues

items.title: Desktop Remote gateway should support switching active Hermes profile from the UI

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

items.body:
## Feature Description

Add a first-class profile switcher for Hermes Desktop when it is connected to a remote Hermes dashboard/TUI backend.

A user should be able to open Hermes Desktop, connect to an existing remote Hermes backend, and switch the active Hermes profile from the Desktop UI, for example:

- `default`
- `crypto`
- `polymarket`
- `mt5`

without manually editing environment variables, restarting services by hand, or changing the Remote URL outside the profile workflow.

## Motivation

Hermes profiles are useful for isolating configs, sessions, memories, skills, SOUL/personality, tools, provider credentials, and domain-specific workspaces. In a common remote setup, Hermes runs durably on a server or workstation, while Hermes Desktop is only a native client.

Today, when Desktop connects to a remote backend, the effective profile is whichever `HERMES_HOME` / `HERMES_PROFILE` the remote dashboard backend process was started with. The Desktop "Profiles" page can list/create/rename/delete profiles, but selecting a profile there does not switch the backend that the chat/TUI/session APIs use.

This creates a gap for multi-profile users:

- Desktop can see profiles, but cannot use them as active execution targets.
- `hermes profile use <name>` or active profile changes do not safely retarget an already-running backend.
- Users must currently run separate dashboard backends per profile and manually change the Remote URL, or restart a backend with different env vars.
- A UI/backend mismatch would be dangerous: the UI might show one profile while sessions/memory/tools are still written under another profile.

Related context:

- #30626 describes the broader problem that long-running gateways are profile-blind / pinned to the boot-time profile and ignore live profile switches.
- #36970 covers first-class remote-client onboarding for existing Hermes instances.
- #31485 discusses production-grade multi-profile gateway supervision.
- #37674 covers Desktop setup adopting existing Hermes Agent/profile installs.

This issue is specifically about the Hermes Desktop UX and backend contract for switching the active profile while using Desktop as a remote client.

## Expected UX

A possible UX:

1. User connects Hermes Desktop to a remote Hermes backend.
2. Desktop shows the current backend profile, e.g. `default`.
3. User opens Profiles or a profile selector in the title/status area.
4. User selects `crypto`, `polymarket`, `mt5`, etc.
5. Desktop reconnects/rebinds to that profile.
6. All chat/TUI/session/config/memory/skill operations now target the selected profile.
7. The UI clearly indicates the active execution profile.

The critical requirement is that the selected profile must match the backend execution context. A visual-only profile switch is worse than no switch because it risks writing conversations, memories, or tool state to the wrong profile.

## Proposed Solution Options

### Option A: Profile-aware remote backend routing

Add backend/API support for profile-aware routing:

- REST endpoints accept a profile selector where appropriate.
- WebSocket `/api/ws` / JSON-RPC handshake includes the selected profile.
- Backend routes session store, memory, config, skills, and tool execution through the selected profile context.
- Desktop stores the selected remote profile and reconnects the WebSocket when it changes.

This is likely the cleanest UX, but it requires careful profile isolation in long-running Python processes.

### Option B: Multi-profile dashboard supervisor + Desktop abstraction

Support a supervisor that manages one dashboard/TUI backend per profile, then let Desktop switch between them as a profile operation.

Example backend mapping:

- `default` -> `http://host:9120`
- `crypto` -> `http://host:9121`
- `polymarket` -> `http://host:9122`
- `mt5` -> `http://host:9123`

Desktop would present this as "Switch profile" rather than making the user manually edit Remote URL. The connection config could store a profile-to-backend map, or discover it from a supervisor endpoint.

This approach has strong isolation because each backend process has its own `HERMES_HOME` / `HERMES_PROFILE`, avoiding mutable process-global state.

### Option C: Explicit backend reload/switch endpoint

Add an admin endpoint such as:

- `POST /api/profile/switch`
- `POST /api/profile/reload`

The backend would reload itself into the requested profile. This is the simplest conceptual model, but may be risky unless every module-level cache/global that depends on `HERMES_HOME`, config, memory, sessions, skills, provider state, etc. is proven to reload safely.

## Safety / Correctness Requirements

- Do not rely on changing `active_profile` on disk alone for an already-running backend.
- Avoid UI/backend mismatch: the profile displayed by Desktop must be the profile used for session writes and tool execution.
- Existing sessions should either remain bound to their original profile or be explicitly closed/forked when switching profiles.
- WebSocket reconnect should expose the active profile in a `gateway.ready`/status payload so Desktop can verify it.
- The remote profile switch path should not require users to use environment-variable overrides such as `HERMES_DESKTOP_REMOTE_URL` / `HERMES_DESKTOP_REMOTE_TOKEN`.
- It should work for a remote Desktop client connected to an existing Hermes instance; it should not require a duplicate local Hermes install.

## Current Workaround

Run one remote dashboard backend per profile on separate ports, then manually change the Desktop Remote URL and reconnect.

Example:

- `default`: `http://host:9120`
- `crypto`: `http://host:9121`
- `polymarket`: `http://host:9122`
- `mt5`: `http://host:9123`

Each backend process is started with profile-specific environment, for example:

```bash
HERMES_HOME=$HOME/.hermes/profiles/crypto \
HERMES_PROFILE=crypto \
hermes dashboard --no-open --tui --host <tailnet-or-lan-ip> --port 9121 --insecure --skip-build
```

This works operationally, but the Desktop UX should make it a profile switch rather than forcing users to understand and edit backend URLs.

## Environment / Scenario

- Hermes Desktop used as a native client on one machine.
- Hermes Agent dashboard/TUI backend runs on a remote Linux host / tailnet address.
- Multiple Hermes profiles exist on the remote host.
- Desktop Remote gateway mode connects successfully to the dashboard backend.
- Desired behavior: switch remote execution profile from within the Desktop app.

### Bug Description

Voice chat / microphone access fails on macOS with Hermes Desktop.

The app never prompts for microphone permission under **System Settings → Privacy & Security → Microphone**, and immediately fails with a message about microphone access being denied.

TCC logs show:
> `Prompting policy for hardened runtime; service: kTCCServiceMicrophone requires entitlement com.apple.security.device.audio-input but it is missing`

The entitlement exists in `apps/desktop/electron/entitlements.mac.plist`, but is **missing from `entitlements.mac.inherit.plist`**, which is what the Electron Helper and Setup processes inherit.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Launch Hermes Desktop on macOS (Apple Silicon).
2. Connect to a gateway (local or remote).
3. Start a voice chat session.
4. App immediately fails with microphone access error. No TCC prompt ever appears.

### Expected Behavior

macOS should prompt for microphone access (or allow it if previously granted). Voice chat should start successfully.

### Actual Behavior

Immediate failure:  
**"Could not start voice session — Microphone access denied."**

The app does not appear in **System Settings → Privacy & Security → Microphone**.  
TCC policy blocks access because the required entitlement is missing on the Helper/Setup binaries.

### Affected Component

Other

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

_No response_

### Debug Report

```shell
Debug report uploaded:
  Report     https://paste.rs/lK5nv
  agent.log  https://paste.rs/fYBLE
```

### Operating System

macOS 26.5.1 (25F80)

### Python Version

3.12.6

### Hermes Version

0.15.1

### Additional Logs / Traceback (optional)

```shell

```

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

The entitlement `com.apple.security.device.audio-input` exists in `entitlements.mac.plist` but is missing from `entitlements.mac.inherit.plist`. Electron Helper processes (and Setup binaries) inherit from the latter file when `hardenedRuntime: true` is enabled in electron-builder. This prevents macOS from showing the TCC microphone prompt.

### Proposed Fix (optional)

Add the following to `apps/desktop/electron/entitlements.mac.inherit.plist`:

```xml
<key>com.apple.security.device.audio-input</key>
<true/>
<key>com.apple.security.device.camera</key>
<true/>
```

Then rebuild the desktop app.

items.title: [Bug]: disk-cleanup can still delete cron/jobs.json from stale tracked.json entries

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

items.body:
## Bug Description

`disk-cleanup` can still delete the cron registry from stale `tracked.json` entries after #32164 / #34840.

#34840 fixed the new classification path by changing `guess_category()` so only `cron/output/**` is treated as `cron-output`. That part looks correct.

The remaining issue is old state. If an older `tracked.json` already contains entries such as:

```text
$HERMES_HOME/cron/jobs.json -> cron-output
$HERMES_HOME/cron -> cron-output
```

then `quick()` still trusts the stored category and deletes those paths once they pass the age threshold. It does not revalidate the path before unlinking or removing it.

This can wipe `$HERMES_HOME/cron/jobs.json`, which removes the live scheduler registry.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Have a stale `tracked.json` entry from before #34840, for example:

   ```json
   {
     "path": "$HERMES_HOME/cron/jobs.json",
     "category": "cron-output",
     "timestamp": "<older than 14 days>",
     "size": 12345
   }
   ```

2. Run a later Hermes version that includes #34840.
3. Trigger `disk-cleanup.quick()`. One normal way this can happen is the plugin's `on_session_end` hook after a test file was tracked.
4. Check `$HERMES_HOME/cron/jobs.json`.

## Expected Behavior

`quick()` should refuse to delete cron control-plane state, even if `tracked.json` contains stale bad entries from an older version.

`cron-output` should only be deletable when the path is still under `$HERMES_HOME/cron/output/**` at delete time.

## Actual Behavior

`quick()` deletes based on the stored category:

```python
should_delete = (
    cat == "test"
    or (cat == "temp" and age > 7)
    or (cat == "cron-output" and age > 14)
)

if should_delete:
    if p.is_file():
        p.unlink()
    elif p.is_dir():
        shutil.rmtree(p)
```

Since the stale entry still says `cron-output`, `jobs.json` can be deleted even though current `guess_category()` would no longer classify it that way.

Sanitized log excerpt:

```text
TRACKED: $HERMES_HOME/cron/jobs.json (cron-output)
TRACKED: $HERMES_HOME/cron (cron-output)
...
DELETED: $HERMES_HOME/cron/jobs.json (cron-output)
DELETED: $HERMES_HOME/cron/output (cron-output)
DELETED: $HERMES_HOME/cron (cron-output)
AUTO_QUICK (session_end): deleted=3 ...
```

## Affected Component

Tools (terminal, file ops, web, code execution, etc.)

More specifically: bundled `disk-cleanup` plugin and cron state handling.

## Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

N/A. The data loss is in local cron state. It can be noticed through gateway cron delivery, but the root problem is not platform-specific.

## Debug Report

Not included because this is a sanitized report. `hermes debug share` would upload local config and recent logs, and this issue only needs the redacted cleanup log excerpt above.

## Operating System

Ubuntu 24.04 on WSL

## Python Version

Python 3.11.15

## Hermes Version

Hermes Agent v0.15.1 (2026.5.29)

The installed checkout was a few commits behind `origin/main`, but the local `plugins/disk-cleanup/disk_cleanup.py` matched current `origin/main` for the relevant code path.

## Additional Logs / Traceback (optional)

```text
TRACKED: $HERMES_HOME/cron/jobs.json (cron-output)
TRACKED: $HERMES_HOME/cron (cron-output)
...
DELETED: $HERMES_HOME/cron/jobs.json (cron-output)
DELETED: $HERMES_HOME/cron/output (cron-output)
DELETED: $HERMES_HOME/cron (cron-output)
AUTO_QUICK (session_end): deleted=3 ...
```

## Root Cause Analysis (optional)

#34840 fixed `guess_category()` around `plugins/disk-cleanup/disk_cleanup.py`, so new tracking skips cron control-plane files:

```python
if top == "cron" or top == "cronjobs":
    if len(rel.parts) >= 2 and rel.parts[1] == "output":
        return "cron-output"
    return None
```

But `quick()` does not call that logic again before deletion. It loads old `tracked.json` state and deletes based on `item["category"]` alone.

That means the classification-time guard works for new entries, but stale bad entries from before #34840 can still delete protected cron state.

## Proposed Fix (optional)

Add delete-time validation in `quick()` before `unlink()` / `rmtree()`.

For `cat == "cron-output"`, only allow deletion when the resolved path is under `$HERMES_HOME/cron/output/**`. If a stale entry points to anything else under `cron` or `cronjobs`, skip it and remove it from `tracked.json` as invalid stale state.

At minimum, these paths should never be deleted by `disk-cleanup`, regardless of stored category:

```text
$HERMES_HOME/cron/jobs.json
$HERMES_HOME/cron/.tick.lock
$HERMES_HOME/cron/
$HERMES_HOME/cronjobs/
```

This is an incomplete fix / stale-state migration issue after #32164 and #34840, not a new misclassification in `guess_category()`.

## Are you willing to submit a PR for this?

Yes

items.title: Windows installer fails with "Access denied" — wipes venv while app + leaked child processes still hold files open

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

items.body:
**Environment:** Windows 11, bootstrap-installer (Tauri) updating an existing install at `%LOCALAPPDATA%\hermes\hermes-agent`.

**Symptom:** Update/reinstall aborts with *"INSTALL DIDN'T FINISH"*:

- `Cannot remove item ...\hermes-agent\venv\Scripts\python.exe: Access to the path 'python.exe' is denied.`
- After clearing that, it fails again on `...\venv\Lib\site-packages\tornado\speedups.pyd`.

**Root cause:** These are *file locks, not permission errors.* Windows won't delete a running `.exe` or a loaded `.pyd`/`.dll` regardless of privilege — running the installer as admin does **not** help. The update step tears down and recreates the venv while files inside it are still open.

**Two distinct lockers observed:**

1. **Leaked child processes from prior runs** — `python -m http.server` (ports 5174 / 4173 / 8765) and `dev_server.py`, still alive *days* later (multiple copies fighting over the same port), all running from `venv\Scripts\python.exe`. These never get reaped on shutdown.
2. **The running `hermes.exe` desktop app itself**, holding `tornado\speedups.pyd` loaded — and it runs elevated, so even a non-elevated `Stop-Process` returns Access denied.

**Repro:** Have the desktop app (or any venv child process) running, then trigger an update/reinstall.

**Workaround (what fixed it for me):**

```powershell
# elevated PowerShell
Stop-Process -Name hermes -Force
Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "Name='python.exe'" |
  Where-Object { $_.ExecutablePath -like '*hermes-agent\venv*' } |
  ForEach-Object { Stop-Process -Id $_.ProcessId -Force }
# then click "Retry install"
```

**Suggested fixes:**

- Stop the running app **and all child processes it spawned** before deleting/replacing the venv.
- Reap leaked children on exit (job object / process group). The `http.server` and `dev_server.py` processes outliving the parent is the underlying leak.
- Use the Restart Manager API to detect the locking PID and prompt "close X" instead of failing generically.
- Fix the error copy so it doesn't imply elevation will help — it's a lock, not an ACL issue.

gateway/platforms/api_server.py:2713-2724
gateway/platforms/api_server.py:2944-2964
agent/redact.py:326-427
tools/mcp_tool.py:315-321,1078

## Technical Reproduction
1. Use the local Hermes checkout at commit `6d5838f9b96fcb73e64772d1e39814ba017b5e3b`; after `git fetch origin main`, the inspected API-server file has no diff from `origin/main`.
2. Configure the API server with a valid API-server bearer token and a provider configuration that deterministically raises an auth or transport exception whose message includes credential-shaped material.
3. Call `/v1/chat/completions` or `/v1/responses` and let the agent call fail before producing a safe assistant response.
4. Observe the API-server code pass `str(e)`, `result.get("error")`, `agent_error`, or traceback-derived text into the HTTP body, SSE payload, assistant content, or response snapshot without redaction.

Centralize API-server error serialization through a forced secret-redaction helper before building OpenAI-compatible error envelopes, streaming events, assistant fallback text, and persisted response snapshots. ## Bug Description

MCP server tools return `"MCP server '<name>' is not connected"` when called from agent context, while `hermes mcp test <name>` shows the server is connected and tools are discovered.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure an HTTP-based MCP server:
```yaml
# ~/.hermes/config.yaml
mcp_servers:
  wechat:
    url: https://changfengbox.top/api/mcp
    connect_timeout: 30
    timeout: 60
```

2. Test the connection:
```
$ hermes mcp test wechat
Testing 'wechat'...
  Transport: HTTP → https://changfengbox.top/api/mcp
  ✓ Connected (927ms)
  ✓ Tools discovered: 2
```

3. Call the tool from agent context:
```
mcp_wechat_wechat(url="...", config={"MD": true})
→ {"error": "MCP server 'wechat' is not connected"}
```

## Expected Behavior

Tool call should succeed since the server is reachable and tools are discovered.

## Actual Behavior

- `hermes mcp list` shows `wechat` as `✓ enabled`
- `hermes mcp test wechat` connects successfully and discovers tools
- Agent tool calls fail with "not connected"

## Root Cause Hypothesis

The connection state check in the agent tool dispatch path uses a different mechanism than `hermes mcp test`. The test command creates a fresh connection, while the agent context may be checking a stale/cached connection state.

## Workaround

Direct HTTP call to the MCP server works:
```bash
curl -s --max-time 30 "https://changfengbox.top/api/mcp" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"wechat","arguments":{"url":"...","config":{"MD":true}}}, "id":1}'
```

## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.15.1 (2026.5.29)
- Python 3.11.2
- Linux 5.10.134

## Bug description
When I open Hermes Desktop and trigger an update from inside the desktop app, the app appears to stay in an "updating" state forever instead of cleanly finishing and returning to a usable UI.

At the same time, the terminal shows this error:

```text
Error occurred in handler for 'hermes:api': Error: connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:9120
    at TCPConnectWrap.afterConnect [as oncomplete] (node:net:1645:16) {
  errno: -111,

```

## Steps to reproduce
1. Launch Hermes Desktop.
2. Use the in-app update flow.
3. Wait for the desktop app to finish updating.
4. Observe that the UI keeps showing an updating/loading state instead of completing normally.
5. Check the terminal that launched Hermes Desktop.

## Expected behavior
After the update finishes, Hermes Desktop should either:
- reconnect automatically to the updated backend and return to the normal UI, or
- clearly prompt for a restart and stop the update flow.

It should not remain in an apparent endless updating state.

## Actual behavior
- The desktop UI appears stuck updating forever.
- The terminal shows `connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:9120` from the `hermes:api` handler.
- Wayland also logs a presentation feedback warning.

## Additional observations
I checked the local Hermes logs after the failure.

`~/.hermes/logs/desktop.log` shows the update itself completing successfully, including these lines:

```text
[hermes] [updates] done: Backend updated. Restart Hermes to load the new version.

```

So from the logs, the update/build path looks successful, but the desktop app UI still ends up stuck while `hermes:api` is trying to connect to `127.0.0.1:9120` and gets `ECONNREFUSED`.

## Environment
- Hermes CLI/Desktop version: `Hermes Agent v0.15.1 (2026.5.29)`
- Desktop package version: `apps/desktop/package.json` = `0.15.1`

items.title: Identified reproducible Hermes MCP issue while configuring n8n MCP server

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

items.body:
## Summary

`hermes mcp add` fails with **401 Unauthorized** when adding an HTTP MCP server that uses header auth with `Authorization: Bearer ${MCP_N8N_API_KEY}`, while `hermes mcp test <name>` succeeds against the same URL and token.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.15.1 (2026.5.29)
- macOS
- MCP server: n8n instance-level MCP at `http://localhost:5678/mcp-server/http`
- Auth: `hermes mcp add <name> --url ... --auth header`
- Token in `~/.hermes/.env` as `MCP_<SERVER>_API_KEY` (JWT only, no `Bearer` prefix)

## Steps to reproduce

1. Set `MCP_N8N_API_KEY=<valid n8n MCP JWT>` in `~/.hermes/.env` (from n8n **Settings → MCP Access**).
2. Run:

   ```bash
   hermes mcp add n8n --url http://localhost:5678/mcp-server/http --auth header
   ```

3. Confirm overwrite if prompted; confirm authentication is required.
4. Observe connection failure during the discovery probe.

## Expected behavior

The discovery probe succeeds (same as `hermes mcp test n8n`), tools are listed, and config is saved.

## Actual behavior

```text
✗ Failed to connect: Client error '401 Unauthorized' for url 'http://localhost:5678/mcp-server/http'
```

Meanwhile:

```bash
hermes mcp test n8n
```

→ **Connected**, tools discovered (e.g. 27 tools for n8n MCP).

## Root cause

`cmd_mcp_add` in `hermes_cli/mcp_config.py` builds a fresh `server_config` with:

```python
server_config["headers"] = {
    "Authorization": f"Bearer ${{{env_key}}}"
}
```

and calls `_probe_single_server(name, server_config)`.

`_probe_single_server` passes that dict to `_connect_server` / `_run_http` **without** resolving `${ENV}` placeholders.

Runtime MCP loading via `_load_mcp_config()` in `tools/mcp_tool.py` **does** call `load_hermes_dotenv()` and `_interpolate_env_vars()`. Config loaded for `hermes mcp test` is also resolved when read through `load_config()`.

So the **add** probe sends the literal header:

```http
Authorization: Bearer ${MCP_N8N_API_KEY}
```

which n8n correctly rejects with 401.

Manual verification with curl:

| Authorization header | HTTP result |
|----------------------|-------------|
| `Bearer ${MCP_N8N_API_KEY}` (literal) | 401 |
| `Bearer <jwt>` | 200 |
| `Bearer Bearer <jwt>` (double prefix) | 401 |

## Proposed fix

In `hermes_cli/mcp_config.py`, resolve env placeholders (and load dotenv) before probing — mirror `_load_mcp_config()` behavior:

```python
def _resolve_mcp_server_config(config: dict) -> dict:
    from hermes_cli.env_loader import load_hermes_dotenv
    from tools.mcp_tool import _interpolate_env_vars

    load_hermes_dotenv()
    return _interpolate_env_vars(config)


def _probe_single_server(name: str, config: dict, connect_timeout: float = 30):
    config = _resolve_mcp_server_config(config)
    ...
```

Optional hardening in `cmd_mcp_add`: strip a leading `Bearer ` from pasted tokens before saving to `MCP_*_API_KEY`, since the header template already adds `Bearer `.

## Related UX / docs issues (same area)

| Issue | Notes |
|-------|--------|
| Wrong config key | `hermes config set mcp.servers.<name>...` writes under `mcp.servers`; runtime reads **`mcp_servers`** (top-level). `hermes mcp list` shows empty until corrected. |
| `hermes config unset` | Not a valid subcommand; CLI reports invalid choice for `unset`. |
| Double `Bearer` | If `MCP_*_API_KEY` is `Bearer <jwt>` and header is `Bearer ${MCP_*_API_KEY}`, n8n receives `Bearer Bearer ...` → 401. |

## Workaround (until fixed)

1. Do **not** re-run `hermes mcp add` if `hermes mcp test <name>` already passes; answer **N** when asked to save config after a failed add.
2. Use top-level **`mcp_servers`** in `~/.hermes/config.yaml` (not `mcp.servers`):

   ```yaml
   mcp_servers:
     n8n:
       url: http://localhost:5678/mcp-server/http
       headers:
         Authorization: Bearer ${MCP_N8N_API_KEY}
       enabled: true
   ```

3. In `~/.hermes/.env`, store **only the JWT** (no `Bearer` prefix):

   ```env
   MCP_N8N_API_KEY=eyJ...
   ```

4. n8n MCP expects `Authorization: Bearer <token>` (see n8n instance-level MCP connection docs).

## Local patch note (not upstream)

A temporary fix was applied locally to `~/.hermes/hermes-agent/hermes_cli/mcp_config.py` (`_resolve_mcp_server_config`, `_strip_bearer_prefix`). **This is overwritten** on `hermes update` or reinstall. User config in `~/.hermes/config.yaml` and `~/.hermes/.env` persists across updates.

## References

- Hermes MCP config key: `mcp_servers` in `~/.hermes/config.yaml` (`hermes_cli/mcp_config.py`, `tools/mcp_tool.py`)
- n8n MCP HTTP endpoint: `/mcp-server/http`
- Cursor MCP example (separate client): `n8n/cursor-mcp.env.example` in this repo

items.title: ACP mode ignores platform_toolsets, causing memory provider tools to be gated out
items.body:
## Summary

In ACP mode, `enabled_toolsets` is hardcoded to `["hermes-acp"]` + MCP servers in `acp_adapter/session.py`. This means `platform_toolsets` configuration (e.g. `cli: [..., "memory", ...]`) is completely ignored. As a result, memory provider tools (e.g. `hindsight_retain`, `hindsight_recall`, `hindsight_reflect`) are silently gated out by the fix in #30177 / #5544, even when the user explicitly enabled the `"memory"` toolset in their config.

## Root Cause

1. `agent_init.py` (post-#30177) gates memory provider tool injection on `enabled_toolsets`:
   ```python
   if agent.enabled_toolsets is None or "memory" in agent.enabled_toolsets:
       # inject memory tools
   ```

2. `acp_adapter/session.py` creates the agent with:
   ```python
   "enabled_toolsets": _expand_acp_enabled_toolsets(
       ["hermes-acp"],           # hardcoded, ignores config
       mcp_server_names=...,
   ),
   ```

3. `_expand_acp_enabled_toolsets` never reads `config.get("platform_toolsets")`.

So `enabled_toolsets` in ACP mode is always `["hermes-acp", "mcp-xxx", ...]` — `"memory"` is never present, and memory tools are always blocked.

## Impact

- **CLI mode**: works correctly. `platform_toolsets.cli` is respected.
- **ACP mode** (VS Code / Zed / JetBrains plugins): memory provider tools are invisible to the model, regardless of `memory_mode` (`hybrid`, `tools`, etc.).
- Auto-recall / prefetch still works (it bypasses the gate), but the model cannot actively call memory tools.

## Minimal Repro

1. Configure hindsight with `memory_mode: "hybrid"` or `"tools"`.
2. Ensure `platform_toolsets.cli` includes `"memory"`.
3. Start a session via ACP (e.g. VS Code extension).
4. Check `agent.log`: `Memory provider 'hindsight' registered (3 tools)` — schemas are returned.
5. But `agent.tools` does not contain `hindsight_retain`/`recall`/`reflect` because the gate filters them out.

## Suggested Fix

In `acp_adapter/session.py`, read `platform_toolsets` from config before constructing `enabled_toolsets`:

```python
platform_toolsets = config.get("platform_toolsets", {})
base_toolsets = (
    platform_toolsets.get("acp")
    or platform_toolsets.get("cli")
    or ["hermes-acp"]
)
"enabled_toolsets": _expand_acp_enabled_toolsets(
    base_toolsets,
    mcp_server_names=configured_mcp_servers,
),
```

## Related

- #5544 — original issue about memory tools leaking
- #30177 — fix that introduced the gate
- PR #5788 — original gate fix by @Lempkey

items.title: Audit ledger: deterministic redacted evidence capture for prompts and tool payloads
items.body:
## Feature description
Add deterministic, local, pre-persistence redaction for audit-ledger evidence capture so Hermes can retain useful prompt/tool evidence without storing raw secrets.

## Motivation
The audit/visibility UI should build trust by showing what Hermes did, why it did it, which tools/paths/domains were involved, and whether actions crossed the machine boundary. Metadata-only records are not enough, but raw prompt/tool logging can leak tokens, cookies, private keys, .env values, and credentials.

## Proposed solution
- Add a local deterministic redaction layer; do not call an LLM for redaction.
- Redact by sensitive key names, HTTP auth/cookie headers, env-style assignments, known secret token patterns, private-key blocks, database/URL credentials, and sensitive query parameters.
- Preserve evidence context where safe: tool name, file paths, commands with secrets masked, domains/schemes, status/exit metadata, prompt/message previews, chars, truncation flags, and hashes.
- Run redaction before persistence/export to any audit sink.
- Keep LLM use optional and downstream only for summaries/classification over already-redacted data.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Redaction helper is pure/local/deterministic and unit tested.
- [ ] Tool args/results and LLM message evidence can include redacted previews plus hashes/truncation metadata.
- [ ] Authorization headers, cookies, API keys/tokens/passwords, .env-style values, private keys, URL credentials, and sensitive query params are masked.
- [ ] Tests prove raw secret values are absent while useful context remains.
- [ ] PR body links this issue and documents test commands.

## Non-goals for first PR
- Full audit UI implementation.
- Sending raw payloads to an LLM for redaction.
- Raw unredacted persistence by default.

### Steps to Reproduce

Install Hermes Desktop on Windows 11
Configure LM Studio as provider (provider: lmstudio, base_url: http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1)

Complete response delivered, same as on Linux/Ubuntu.


### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

On Windows, Python's asyncio uses ProactorEventLoop (I/O completion ports) instead of SelectorEventLoop (epoll/kqueue) used on Linux. ProactorEventLoop has known issues with HTTPX streaming connections — when the connection is closed during an active stream, it raises RuntimeError('Event loop is closed') instead of handling the close gracefully.

This is not a LM Studio issue — the same LM Studio server works fine when accessed from:

Hermes on Ubuntu 24.04
Other HTTP clients (curl, Postman, browser)
Hermes Desktop connected to remote providers (OpenRouter, DeepSeek)

### Proposed Fix (optional)

Force asyncio to use SelectorEventLoop on Windows, or add a try/except around the HTTPX stream close to handle RuntimeError('Event loop is closed') gracefully. Example workaround:

import asyncio
import selectors
if hasattr(selectors, 'PollSelector'):
    asyncio.set_event_loop_policy(asyncio.WindowsSelectorEventLoopPolicy())

items.title: feat(desktop): support local and remote Hermes backends simultaneously
items.body:
## Feature Description

Add support in Hermes Desktop for connecting to both a local Hermes backend and one or more remote Hermes backends at the same time.

Today the Desktop gateway settings are mutually exclusive: the app is either in `local` mode or `remote` mode. That makes sense for a first version, but it prevents using the Desktop as a single control surface for multiple agents/backends — for example, keeping the local MacBook agent available while also monitoring/controlling a remote Hermes agent running on another machine.

## Motivation

Users may run Hermes in multiple places:

- a local Desktop/CLI agent on their personal machine
- a remote always-on agent/server
- specialized remote profiles or work machines
- multiple agent backends for different projects or environments

The Desktop UI would be much more useful as a multi-agent control panel if local and remote targets could coexist instead of forcing a global switch.

## Current Behavior

In the current Desktop implementation:

- `GatewaySettings` models the connection as a single `mode: 'local' | 'remote'`.
- The UI shows two exclusive cards: "Local gateway" and "Remote gateway".
- `connection.json` stores one selected mode and one remote URL/token.
- `startHermes()` resolves a single backend:
  - if remote is selected, connect to remote and do not start local
  - otherwise start a private localhost backend
- `Save and reconnect` resets the single connection and reloads the window.
- Renderer API calls route through a single active `startHermes()` connection.

Relevant files:

- `apps/desktop/src/app/settings/gateway-settings.tsx`
- `apps/desktop/electron/main.cjs`
- `apps/desktop/src/global.d.ts`

## Proposed Solution

Introduce multi-backend / workspace-style connection management in Desktop:

1. Allow the app to keep a local backend and remote backend(s) configured simultaneously.
2. Add a backend switcher in the Desktop shell, e.g. "Local", "Remote: server-name", etc.
3. Let sessions, status, agents/subagents, terminal/files, and settings be scoped to the selected backend.
4. Preserve the current single-backend mode as the default/simple path.
5. Optionally allow several remote backends, not just one.

Possible config shape:

```json
{
  "activeBackendId": "local",
  "backends": [
    { "id": "local", "type": "local", "label": "Local MacBook", "enabled": true },
    { "id": "remote-prod", "type": "remote", "label": "Remote server", "url": "https://...", "token": "..." }
  ]
}
```

The main process could manage a map of backend connections rather than a single `connectionPromise` / `hermesProcess`, and the renderer IPC/API calls could accept a backend id or derive it from UI state.

## Alternatives Considered

- Open multiple Desktop app instances, one per backend. This may work as a workaround, but it is not a good UX and does not provide a unified view.
- Keep using the browser dashboard for one backend and Desktop for another. This works but defeats the purpose of Desktop as the control surface.

## Acceptance Criteria

- User can have local and remote gateway configs saved at the same time.
- Switching to a remote backend does not delete/disable the local backend configuration.
- User can switch the active backend from the Desktop UI without manually re-entering tokens.
- Existing single-local behavior remains the default and continues to work offline.
- Remote token storage remains secure via the existing keychain/secret handling.
- The UI clearly indicates which backend a session/action targets.
